text: Nine chapters of this course have each surfaced one real divergence between dialects. This lesson pulls together the five that cause the most actual production bugs when a query crosses platforms, so you have one checklist to run before anything ships -- not nine separate things to remember, just five.

First: NULL versus empty string isn't the same everywhere. On Oracle, inserting an empty string into a VARCHAR2 column doesn't store an empty string at all -- it stores NULL, at the storage level, with no way around it. On T-SQL, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, that same insert stores a real empty string, a value that is explicitly NOT NULL. So a check like WHERE Notes equals empty string, which works fine on T-SQL, silently matches nothing at all on Oracle, because NULL never equals empty string on any platform. The fix on Oracle is always WHERE notes IS NULL instead.

Second: MySQL's historical leniency on type coercion. Older MySQL, in a loose sql_mode, would silently accept things like a zero date, or compare a string column straight against a number without complaint. MySQL has genuinely tightened this -- strict mode has been part of the default sql_mode since version 5.7 -- but plenty of real production databases still run on a looser setting inherited from an older install. Check the actual sql_mode on the actual version in front of you. Don't assume today's defaults apply everywhere.

Third: quoted identifiers fold case differently. Oracle and PostgreSQL fold an unquoted identifier to a fixed case automatically -- uppercase on Oracle, lowercase on PostgreSQL. Quote it instead, to preserve the exact mixed case from a SQL Server script, and now you have to match that exact case on every single reference to that object, forever. T-SQL and MySQL don't fold case this way by default -- this is Lesson 15's material, showing up again at migration time, where it actually bites.

Fourth and fifth, quickly: date and time range and precision differences -- re-check Chapter 2's limits specifically at migration time, because a value that was perfectly valid on the source platform is not guaranteed to be valid, or to round the same way, on the target. And fifth, the one from last lesson: automated tools translate basic syntax well, but they do not reliably translate procedural logic -- TRY CATCH, PL/SQL packages, cursors are different enough across platforms, from Chapters 5 through 8, that no tool can safely guess the right rewrite every time. Budget real human review time for every procedural object, every migration, with no exceptions.

Five items, one checklist: NULL versus empty string, type coercion leniency, case-folding on quoted identifiers, date and time range and precision, and procedural code always needing a human. Each one traces straight back to an earlier chapter in this course. Next lesson is the capstone: one real T-SQL reporting query, translated correctly into three other dialects, side by side, proving everything this course has built toward in one worked example. See you there.
